analysis.one_liner: Gives hourly workers a right to request schedule changes and requires two weeks' advance notice of schedules.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 17, 2025 with 54 cosponsors, all Democrats, and referred to four House committees, where it has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The Schedules That Work Act would let any employee ask their employer for changes to hours, shift times, or work location, and employers would have to discuss the request in good faith and grant it when a worker cites a serious health condition, caregiving, school, or a second job, unless the employer has a real business reason to say no. Workers in retail, food service, cleaning, hotels, and warehouses would also get work schedules at least two weeks in advance, extra pay when their employer changes the schedule with less notice or cuts a scheduled shift, and the right to decline shifts starting less than 11 hours after their last one. The bill bans retaliation for using these rights and lets workers sue or complain to the Labor Department.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers in retail, food service, cleaning, hotels, and warehouses, who today often learn their schedules a week or less in advance, get shifts cancelled at the last minute, and work back-to-back closing and opening shifts. Caregivers, people managing health conditions, students, and people working second jobs gain a right to ask for steadier hours without fear of being punished for asking.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly retail, food, and warehouse workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers to give covered sector workers their schedules at least 14 days ahead, in writing, and pay $75 per day of notice missed; changes to a posted schedule require 14 days' notice or extra 'predictability pay.'

Entitles workers to extra pay when the employer adds or moves a shift with less than 14 days' notice, half pay for scheduled hours the employer cancels, one extra hour of pay per split-shift day, and 1.5 times pay for shifts worked less than 11 hours after the previous shift.

Requires an employer to engage in a good-faith discussion about a schedule request and, for requests tied to serious health conditions, caregiving, career education, or a second job, to grant the request unless it has a bona fide business reason to deny it.

Makes it unlawful to fire, demote, cut hours of, or otherwise retaliate against a worker for requesting a schedule change or exercising any right under the bill, with damages, reinstatement, and attorney's fees available in court and civil penalties of $500 to $5,000 for willful, repeated violations.

Requires employers to post schedules where all covered workers can see them, lets workers decline without penalty to work hours not on their posted schedule, and requires an annual written estimate of each worker's minimum monthly hours.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees in the covered sectors, mainly large retail, restaurant, hotel, cleaning, and warehouse companies, which would bear the cost of predictability and split-shift pay, advance scheduling, and recordkeeping, and would lose the staffing flexibility of last-minute schedule changes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large retail, restaurant, hotel, and warehouse employers

drawbacks.text: The pay premiums and 14-day notice rules raise operating costs for employers, who may respond by hiring fewer workers, cutting hours, or raising prices, and the bill applies to employers with as few as 15 employees, reaching many small businesses in the covered sectors.

Unionized workplaces can be exempted if a collective bargaining agreement governs scheduling and expressly waives the bill's provisions, so nonunion workers get protections that some union members may sign away.

The 'bona fide business reason' standard for denying requests, covering everything from customer demand to business performance, is broad enough that employers could deny many requests, and the law's effect would depend heavily on how the Labor Department writes regulations and how courts apply the standard.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — stable, predictable schedules for hourly workers who currently get little notice and lose pay to last-minute cancellations — addresses a real, well-documented hardship, and the bill follows rules already adopted by Oregon and ten municipalities cited in its findings [S2]. The costs are real but fall on large, labor-intensive employers with scheduling flexibility, and the bill's own findings note a Gap Inc. experiment found stable schedules raised store productivity and sales [S2]. The main design weaknesses are the small 15-employee coverage threshold, the broad exceptions employers can use to deny requests, and the union waiver carve-out.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to four House committees in December 2025 and no committee has taken it up since; with no final vote yet and the 119th Congress still sitting, it remains parked at the first step.

narrative.text: Representative Rosa DeLauro introduced the Schedules That Work Act in the House on December 17, 2025.
Fifty-four House members, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

The Speaker referred the bill to four committees at once — Education and Workforce, House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary — a multi-committee referral that means several committees would each need to act before the bill can move.
No committee has reported the bill, held a hearing or markup on it, or scheduled it for a floor vote; the only actions on record are the introduction and referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large retail, restaurant, hotel, and warehouse employers keep the current system of short-notice, changeable schedules at no added cost; hourly workers get no new protections.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original or subsequent cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: All 54 sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the committees that hold the bill are chaired by Republicans who have taken no action.

industries.note: Retail is explicitly covered: stores must post schedules 14 days ahead, pay premiums for last-minute changes and cancelled shifts, and pay a split-shift premium. The industry's interest in keeping just-in-time scheduling runs directly against the workers' interest in predictable hours.
Covered sector employers must give two weeks' notice, pay for short-notice changes, and honor 11-hour rest gaps — costs that fall heaviest on chains that rely on on-call and clopening shifts.
Warehouse employees are a named covered group and would gain notice, predictability pay, and rest-period rights that limit last-minute schedule shuffling.
Hospitality establishments are covered; cleaning staff and hourly hotel workers would get steady schedules and premiums, which the industry currently avoids through volatile scheduling.
Cleaning occupations are a covered sector under the bill, subjecting these employers to the notice, predictability pay, and rest requirements.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in four House committees with no recorded action beyond referral. With Republicans holding 223 of 435 House seats, no Republican cosponsors, and a late-session introduction, the likely path is that it never gets a committee markup or floor vote and dies when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, unless sponsors attach it to a larger package or the chamber's composition changes.
